passage:
Payal's report card lay open on the sofa. "Eighty-eight in science," said Papa Yogesh, tapping it. "Where did the other twelve go?" Mummy Deepika nodded and asked to see the test paper. Neither of them mentioned the drawing Payal had done of the water cycle, which her teacher had stuck on the class board. Payal watched their faces. She had learned that they lit up for a number.
That night at her desk, Payal wrote her spelling homework and got one letter wrong. She rubbed it out and wrote it again. The eraser rubbed a hole, then the page tore along the line. "It's ruined!" she whispered, tears dropping on the notebook. She pushed it under her bed instead of handing it in. In the morning the teacher noticed her red eyes. "A torn page is not a failure," the teacher said. "Mistakes are how we work out what to learn next. Bring me the notebook and we will fix it together."
Payal slowly pulled it out.

qa.q: What happened to the page when Payal rubbed out her wrong letter?
qa.a: The eraser rubbed a hole, then the page tore along the line.

qa.q: How do the scene with the report card and the torn notebook page fit together?
qa.a: Her parents reacted only to a number, and Payal had learned they lit up for marks. That is why one wrong letter felt ruined, and she tore the page and pushed the notebook under her bed.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she whispered "It's ruined!"?
qa.a: She felt frightened and ashamed, because a small error seemed to mean she had failed completely.

qa.q: What could Papa Yogesh and Mummy Deepika do differently when a report card comes home?
qa.a: They could first say something warm about her drawing or effort, then talk about what she found hard, so Payal knows their love does not hinge on a score.

grounding: A child whose parents react only to marks (4097) shows tears and torn paper over small mistakes (4429); the same child.
